title: Handle Octopus Numbers With Care
paragraphs: Few animals invite as many superlatives as the octopus, yet the most repeated claims about it deserve a careful second look. That sentence may sound cautious, but it reflects how science actually works: claims are kept when several sources agree. It makes a good test case for reading popular science. That it has three hearts is well established: two pump blood through the gills, while the third circulates it around the body. Reports add that the body heart stops beating while the animal swims, which may help explain why octopuses usually prefer to crawl.

Its blue blood is equally well documented. The colour comes from hemocyanin, a copper-based protein that carries oxygen; human blood uses the iron-based hemoglobin instead. Hemocyanin appears to work well in cold, low-oxygen water, so the blood may reflect the animal's habitat as much as its ancestry. None of this is a substitute for direct measurement; it simply shows that the same fact can be read in more than one way.

The popular claim that an octopus has nine brains is different. It compresses a real observation, namely that most of the animal's neurons sit in its arms, into a slogan. Estimates of the proportion vary: PBS gives about two thirds, while other sources cite lower percentages for the arms. The lesson is not that the slogan is false, but that a memorable number can travel much further than the evidence behind it. Readers who want to repeat an octopus fact would do well to name the source and the date.
